# Panel Seat: Visual Feedback Agent for the Advertisement Studio

## 1. What this decision actually hinges on

Four facts in the evidence do most of the work:

1. **The canvas is already structured.** We have object IDs, types, text strings, fonts, colours, bboxes, z-order. A multimodal model should never have to OCR "Refill. Roam. Repeat." or guess the price — we send those as data. The image is for what metadata can't say: how it *looks* (salience, balance, whether the headline dies against the cup's lid — which, from the screenshot, it plausibly does).
2. **A deterministic layer can compute several techniques locally.** Contrast ratios, whitespace coverage, font counts, hierarchy ladders, quadrant occupancy are cheap pure functions over Fabric objects plus a downscaled bitmap. These facts ground the model (less hallucination), shrink the model we need (cost), and double as the offline fallback (resilience requirement).
3. **Cost is not the binding constraint; latency, reliability and pedagogy are.** Rough maths below show a class session costs tens of cents on Flash-tier models. Even a premium model costs a few dollars per class. So "cheap model" is a preference, not a necessity — calibration should decide, and escalation is economically safe.
4. **Object-anchored feedback beats pixel-anchored feedback.** Cheap VLMs are unreliable at bounding-box coordinates. They are very reliable at referencing IDs from a closed list we provide. The editor can then pulse the actual Fabric object. We get reliable "highlight the thing being discussed" for free, and skip a whole failure class.

One screenshot detail with architectural consequence: the exported snapshot must strip selection chrome (the active-object handles visible in the image). Verify in slice 1 that the export discards active selection first.

## 2. Options

**O1 — Free-chat vision tutor.** Chat box; each message attaches the canvas image; full transcript resent each turn.
Cost: token growth is unbounded (transcript + image per turn); moderation surface; highest build simplicity. Fails: blank-prompt problem for Year 10 ("is this good?" → generic answers); explicitly the "generic tutor" the brief excludes; no technique coverage. Falsifier: pilot logs show >50% of asks are low-content questions and feedback rarely references canvas specifics.

**O2 — One-tap stateless general critic.** Single button; payload = image + product brief; one prompt; no memory.
Cost: cheapest to build and run; single codepath. Fails: OCR dependence for small text; hallucinated objects; repeats itself across revisions; no coverage of the 11 techniques; no fallback value. Falsifier: calibration detection <70% on typography/negative-space flaws, or near-identical responses across consecutive revisions.

**O3 — Technique-picker scoped checks.** Student picks from 11 technique chips; technique-specific rubric prompt per check.
Cost: 11 rubrics to author and maintain (they're data, not code — manageable); request cost same as O2. Fails: choice paralysis; students often don't know which technique is their problem; box-ticking incentive that nudges toward cramming — the opposite of the restraint requirement. Falsifier: usage logs show 2–3 techniques absorb >70% of asks (coverage fails anyway), or ask rate collapses after first use.

**O4 — AIDA-stage-bound critic.** Four modes wired to the existing stage chips/drawer.
Cost: low; natural progressive-disclosure fit. Fails: stage ≠ technique — contrast matters at every stage; a student in Interest may never get typography examined; lockstep conflicts with "ask at any point." Falsifier: stage prompts underperform technique rubrics on seeded-flaw detection in calibration.

**O5 — Facts-first hybrid critic (recommended core).** Client computes visual facts deterministically; request = downscaled image + object metadata + facts + brief + bounded memory; one engine with a focus parameter (auto-prioritised by default; technique/stage/question overrides); responses reference object IDs; local analyzer doubles as offline fallback.
Cost: highest build cost (~3 client modules + function + rubric pack); per-request cost similar to O2 (facts add ~150 tokens, save image resolution). Fails: analyzer bugs produce wrong facts → confidently wrong feedback; auto-prioritisation may pick the wrong focus. Falsifiers: (a) the "image+objects+facts" calibration cell fails to beat "image-only" by ≥10 points on detection/false-flag → drop the facts layer; (b) auto mode identifies the seeded worst-flaw <60% of the time → force technique picker as default.

**O6 — Deterministic-only coach.** Rule-based tips from metadata/facts; no model.
Cost: near-zero marginal cost, zero latency, fully private, works offline. Fails by construction as the feature: cannot read photographs, AI-generated product art, leading lines, realism — i.e., cannot "examine the actual image." Correctly positioned as the degradation layer inside O5, not the product.

**O7 — Premium-model variant of O5** (GPT-4o / Claude-class as the single model).
Cost: ~10–20× per request — roughly $1.50–4 per class session vs ~$0.15; +1–3s latency. Same architecture; a config value, not a redesign. Fails: latency; budget creep at scale; overkill if Flash-tier passes gates. Falsifier: calibration shows Flash-tier passes all acceptance gates → premium unnecessary; keep as the documented escalation path.

**O8 — Deferred/batch critique** at save or stage boundaries.
Cost: fewer calls, smoothed concurrency. Fails: breaks "inside the making loop" — feedback arrives after decisions have hardened. Reject as primary; acceptable later as a revision-summary artifact. Falsifier: pilot metric "% of asks followed by an edit within 60s" is materially higher on-demand than at boundaries (expect it to be).

**O9 — Model-generated region boxes** (draw rings where the model points).
Cost: same requests; adds overlay renderer. Fails: cheap VLMs' pixel coordinates are unreliable, especially small objects; a wrong highlight actively misleads a 15-year-old. Deferred. Adoption test: calibration measures IoU ≥0.5 on ≥90% of referenced objects; current expectation is failure. Object-ID anchoring (O5) captures most of the value reliably.

**O10 — Audience-persona mode** ("focus group of one": model reacts as the defined audience).
Cost: same pipe, different prompt. Fails as a standalone: persona voice crowds out technique precision; risks role-play fluff. Folded into O5 as the mandatory first field of every response ("3-second read: what your audience gets"). Falsifier for keeping it: teacher specificity ratings show the read-of-ad line is less actionable than observations.

**O11 — On-device VLM** (WebGPU in Safari).
Cost: zero marginal cost, private, offline. Fails now: Safari WebGPU constraints on school MacBooks, multi-GB model download over school wifi, thermal variance, quality below the cheap API tier. Reject; revisit in ~2 years.

## 3. Ranking

| Rank | Option | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **O5 facts-first hybrid** | Recommended; absorbs O6 (fallback), O3/O4 (focus overrides), O10 (read-of-ad field) |
| 2 | O7 premium variant | One-line escalation of O5 if calibration fails; economically safe |
| 3 | O3 technique picker | Correct as an *override mode* inside O5, weak as the whole design |
| 4 | O2 one-tap stateless | Acceptable only as a time-boxed first ship; plan to upgrade |
| 5 | O4 stage-bound | Fold stage into focus parameter; insufficient alone |
| 6 | O8 deferred | Secondary artifact at most |
| 7 | O9 region boxes | Defer behind calibration gate |
| 8 | O10 standalone persona | Fold in as a response field |
| 9 | O6 standalone | Fallback layer only |
| 10 | O1 free-chat tutor | Rejected (brief explicitly excludes; unbounded cost/context) |
| 11 | O11 on-device | Rejected for now |

## 4. Recommended architecture (staged)

**Slice 1 (ship first):** one-tap critic, focus = auto or technique chip; payload = image (≤896px JPEG q≈0.7, selection discarded) + capped object list + facts + brief; single Flash-tier model via OpenRouter; schema-validated response; object-pulse on refs; cooldown + change-gating; local analyzer tips as fallback; teacher on/off via env-var flag; metrics logging (no images). No free text, no second model, no diff memory yet.

**Slice 2:** free-text question field (≤280 chars), fallback model route, revision-diff memory, coverage passport with gentle nudges ("you haven't tested negative space yet"), per-class teacher setting.

**Slice 3 (gated on calibration + pilot):** region highlights/crops for typography checks, premium model for auto mode if Flash fails prioritisation, persona emphasis.

**Key mechanisms:**

- **Memory without unbounded context.** Each response ends with a `stateNote` (≤40 tokens, model-written: agreed focus + what to check next). Next request carries that note plus a structural diff computed from the existing object-command history ("headline fontSize 24→32; price tag added") plus an ask counter. Nothing else. No transcripts, ever.
- **Spam and budget hygiene.** Ask allowed only if (a) ≥8s since last ask and (b) image hash or object diff changed — otherwise: "Nothing changed since the last look. Try a move, then ask again." Server-side per-session cap (~20 asks) and class-level hourly cap with honest "critic is busy — retry in a few seconds."
- **Anti-cramming by design.** System prompt explicitly values restraint and licenses the model to recommend *removing* elements; it is forbidden from suggesting a technique merely to increase coverage. The coverage passport tracks *encounters*, not uses. Gallery criteria remain independent of technique count.
- **What the model may not produce.** No rewritten headlines or copy; no scores or grades; no layout dictation. Suggestions name a lever on *their* elements ("increase contrast between o7 and the lid — darker fill or a light plate behind it") phrased as options or questions, max two. Authorship stays with the student because the model never produces final text or pixels.
- **Observation / interpretation / suggestion separation.** Schema-enforced: observations cite object refs and carry a confidence tag; interpretation is one audience-effect clause tied to a technique; suggestions are reversible moves. Low confidence renders with a visible "not sure" tag and names what couldn't be told ("I can't tell if the small text is the price").
- **Placement.** The drawer is already dense. Ask button lives at the drawer bottom (in the making flow, beside the lock-in control); responses render in a collapsible ~270px right panel under the AIDA chips so the canvas and instructions stay visible; object refs in the response pulse the corresponding Fabric object (respecting `prefers-reduced-motion`: static outline instead). First use shows a one-line coach mark; nothing afterwards. Responses are capped at a 3-second read + 2 observations + 2 suggestions + 1 "next move" line, aria-live announced, keyboard navigable, Year-7 reading level.

**Economics (Flash-tier, per request):** system+rubric ~700 cached + schema ~150 + objects ~350 + facts ~120 + brief ~90 + memory ~70 + image ~600–700 ≈ 2,100 input tokens; output capped 280. ≈ **$0.0003–0.0005/request**. A 30-student class at ~12 asks each ≈ **$0.15–0.20 per session**. Even a full premium model stays under ~$4/class. State this plainly to whoever owns the budget: reliability engineering matters more than model price.

**Latency budget:** client timeout 18s with a progress note at 8s; server: primary model 8s → fallback model 5s → fail; one automatic retry on 429/5xx with jitter; total ≤14s. p95 target ≤8s under school-wifi variance. Concurrency of 30 simultaneous asks is trivial for OpenRouter + Flash-tier rate limits; Netlify concurrency is not a concern at this scale.

**Seams (matching the stated architecture):** new client module `studio-feedback/` — `canvasSnapshot.ts` (export + downscale via existing canvas adapter; **must verify account-scoped assets are CORS-clean or `toDataURL` throws**), `visualFacts.ts` (pure, unit-testable), `feedbackClient.ts` (AbortController timeout, dedupe hash, cooldown), `feedbackMemory.ts` (stateNote + diff from object commands). One Netlify Function `studio-feedback` (POST) + `studio-feedback/status` (GET, for teacher flag). Dev seam: recorded-response mock, since Vite preview doesn't serve functions. No DB mutation required for slice 1.

**Generalisability without premature abstraction:** three clean seams only — (1) technique rubrics as a data pack (JSON), (2) the facts extractor as pure functions over a generic object list, (3) a `VisualCritic` provider port with schema-validated I/O. Game-specifics (AIDA, audience signal, persona voice) are config. That *is* the reusable skill later; no plugin infrastructure now.

## 5. End-to-end interaction loop

1. Student (Action stage, per screenshot) taps **"Second pair of eyes"** at drawer bottom. First time: one coach line.
2. Focus row defaults to "Biggest thing holding this ad back"; chips offer current stage + 3 stage-relevant techniques ("more" reveals all 11). Collapsed question field (slice 2).
3. Client checks: status enabled → cooldown → canvas changed. Snapshot: discard selection, export ≤896px JPEG, hash it, collect ≤40 objects (text ≤200 chars each), compute facts.
4. POST with 18s abort. Panel shows "Looking at your ad…"; canvas stays fully interactive.
5. Server: validate → flag → rate bucket → assemble prompt (cached static prefix: persona, untrusted-content rule, schema, full-rubric one-liners + focused rubric in full) → OpenRouter primary → fallback once → schema validate → one repair retry.
6. Panel renders: **3-second read** (audience framing); ≤2 observations with "show" pulse buttons and confidence tags; ≤2 suggestions as options/questions; one "next move" line.
7. Student edits; re-ask gated on change. Model receives `stateNote` + diff and can acknowledge progress ("headline contrast improved; the price is now the quietest element").
8. Failures: timeout → "The critic is stuck (wifi). Your local checks meanwhile:" + deterministic tips + retry button. Teacher-disabled → button replaced by local tips card + "AI eyes are off for this class." Flow never blocks.

## 6. Request/response contract

```json
// POST /studio-feedback  (body hard-capped ~1.2MB)
{
  "v": 1,
  "sessionId": "uuid",            // game session; no alias, no PII
  "revision": 42,
  "focus": { "mode": "auto|technique|stage|question",
             "technique": "negative_space?", "stage": "action?",
             "question": "≤280 chars?" },
  "brief": { "product": "Orbit Tumbler", "audience": "Time after the school day ends.",
             "price": 6.5, "valueProp": "…", "stage": "action" },
  "image": { "mime": "image/jpeg", "data": "base64…", "w": 896, "h": 520, "hash": "sha256:…" },
  "objects": [ { "id": "o7", "type": "text", "text": "Refill. Roam. Repeat.",
                 "fontFamily": "…", "fontSize": 28, "fontWeight": "700",
                 "fill": "#1b1b1b", "bboxPct": [0.31, 0.49, 0.32, 0.17], "z": 3, "angle": 0 } ],
  "facts": { "coveragePct": 31, "fontCount": 3, "largestRef": "o3",
             "contrast": [ { "refA": "o7", "refB": "o3", "ratio": 2.1 } ],
             "quadrantOccupancy": [0,1,0, 1,1,0, 0,0,0] },
  "memory": { "stateNote": "≤40 tok", "diff": "≤60 words", "askCount": 3 }
}
```

```json
// 200 response
{ "v": 1, "status": "ok",
  "readOfAd": "≤25 words — what your audience gets in 3 seconds",
  "observations": [ { "text": "…", "refs": ["o7"], "confidence": "high|low" } ],   // ≤2, refs ⊆ objects
  "suggestions":  [ { "move": "…", "why": "…", "refs": ["o7"], "kind": "option|question" } ], // ≤2, no copy
  "nextFocus": "negative_space",
  "stateNote": "≤40 tokens",
  "usage": { "in": 0, "out": 0 }, "model": "…", "latencyMs": 0 }

// error: { "status": "disabled|busy|unavailable|invalid", "retryAfterMs": 0 }
// fallback tips are computed client-side from facts — no server dependency.
```

Validator drops unknown refs, grade-like content, and any suggestion containing replacement copy patterns; one repair retry, then safe failure.

## 7. Minimum viable calibration plan

- **Fixtures:** 48 Fabric fixtures (JSON + rendered PNG): 11 techniques × {done well, flawed, absent} = 33, plus 9 edge cases — text-over-image low contrast (mirrors the current screenshot), near-empty canvas, crowded, two focal points, illegible price, injected canvas text ("ignore your instructions…"), off-topic image, oversized object count, non-ad.
- **Gold labels:** two human raters label per-technique pass/concern and "what most limits this ad"; report inter-rater agreement; adjudicate disagreements.
- **Matrix:** 3 models (Gemini Flash-tier, GPT-4o-mini, one open-vision floor e.g. Qwen-VL) × 3 payloads (image-only / +objects / +objects+facts) × 2 runs ≈ 864 calls, **< $2 compute**, 2–3 days effort.
- **Gates:** seeded-flaw detection ≥80% on high-severity; **false-flag rate ≤15% (the kill metric — confident wrong feedback is pedagogically worse than none)**; schema-valid ≥97% first attempt, ≥99.5% after repair; ref-validity 100%; p95 ≤8s; injection fixtures never produce instruction-breaking output.
- **Decision rule:** cheapest passing cell wins. If none passes: (a) test premium model on auto mode only; (b) narrow to technique-scoped mode (drop auto prioritisation) and re-test. This is the explicit falsification path for the whole design.
- **Pilot:** one class, one session, logged (no images): ask→edit-within-60s rate (target ≥50%), repeat-ask rate, technique coverage, timeout/disable rate, teacher debrief on specificity/authorship.

## 8. First implementation slice

1. `canvasSnapshot.ts` + `visualFacts.ts` (pure functions; unit tests incl. CORS-taint and selection-chrome checks).
2. `studio-feedback` function: auto+technique focus, single model, Zod schema, env-flag, code-only failures.
3. Drawer button + right panel: response card, object pulse, cooldown/change gating, local tips fallback card.
4. `stateNote` round-trip memory only (diff in slice 2).
5. Recorded-response mock for Vite preview; metrics logging without images.
Acceptance: works with AI flag off; p95 ≤8s on throttled network; response renders correctly on the screenshot's exact canvas state.

## 9. Safety, privacy, integrity — and risks stated plainly

- **Injection:** all canvas text and the question field are treated as untrusted data (delimited, system-prompt rule, schema-bound output, plain-text rendering). Blast radius is the injecting student's own screen; fixtures test it anyway.
- **Privacy:** no alias, no PII; images transient; logs are metrics only. **Unverified assumption: OpenRouter provider no-training/data terms satisfy school policy — someone must confirm before any student pixels leave the device.**
- **Integrity:** feedback is process aid, never assessment evidence; no scores exist in the schema; gallery criteria are untouched.
- **Teacher control:** env flag in slice 1; **per-class toggle requires a settings read path the panel can't see — if that needs DB mutation it's a declared dependency outside this scope, and it blocks classroom ship.**
- **Real risks, unsoftened:** cheap VLMs may genuinely fail spatial judgments (leading lines, negative space) — facts help but may not close the gap; a buggy facts layer makes the model *confidently* wrong; Safari canvas taint from one mis-configured asset kills export silently; one student can still burn budget clicking without the caps; model IDs on OpenRouter deprecate — pin and config-drive them.

**Assumptions the design makes:** ≤35 students/class, ~12 asks each; role-swapping implies possibly one MacBook per pair (halves concurrency — worst case designed for); OpenRouter billing already exists via the image lab; canvas assets are same-origin/CORS-clean; students read short Year-7-level text; session log lives client-side via existing persistence (no DB mutation); env-var flag is acceptable for v1.

## Terminal recommendation

Build **O5 staged**: facts-first hybrid critic — downscaled image + structured objects + deterministic facts + brief + self-compressing memory, one engine with an auto-prioritised focus and technique/stage/question overrides, object-anchored schema-bound responses, local analyzer as the offline/teacher-off fallback, Flash-tier model with a documented one-line premium escalation, ship gated on the calibration matrix and one-class pilot.

**Confidence: 7/10.** High on the architecture (every constraint in the brief points at it); medium on cheap-model adequacy for spatial technique judgment — that is exactly what the calibration plan exists to decide, and the design already contains its own fallback if the answer is no.
message.reasoning:
Let me think carefully about this task. I'm an independent seat on a blind design panel. I need to design viable options for a custom in-canvas visual feedback agent for a Year 10 advertising design studio, stress-test them, rank them, and produce a recommended architecture with concrete artifacts: interaction flow, request/response contract, calibration plan, first implementation slice. I should be concrete, not soften risks, not pad.

Key constraints from the brief:

- Year 10 students (age ~15-16), pairs, MacBooks, Safari, school wifi.
- Godot 4 game with embedded TypeScript/Fabric.js ad studio in verified web export. Netlify Functions for hosted routes. OpenRouter default model substrate.
- The agent: at any point in the individual ad stage, student asks it to examine the actual canvas image; responds with targeted ideas/feedback grounded in the actual image. Student edits, asks again. Inside the making loop. Helps use AIDA and visual techniques deliberately without taking authorship away.
- Low per-use cost, low latency, resilience on school wifi. Whole class (~30 students, ~15 pairs... but ads are individual, so up to ~30 concurrent users) may use simultaneously.
- AI availability teacher-controlled. If AI unavailable, ad-making flow remains usable.
- No PII needed. Aliases exist but model doesn't need personal info.
- Technique set: salience, colour, contrast, leading lines, framing, negative space, depth and layers, rule of odds, juxtaposition, typography, visual hierarchy. Students must encounter all, but not rewarded for cramming.
- Onboarding doctrine: progressive disclosure. Only instruction needed for current action. Fun-first. Avoid assignment framing.
- Current evidence: screenshot shows the studio. The drawer on the left (~230px) shows AIDA Action-stage cards. Canvas mostly empty; cup line drawing ~180x250 center; selected text "Refill. Roam. Repeat." crosses the cup. AIDA chips top right (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action). Tool rail far left: Build, Assets, Words, Logo, Image, Price, AIDA. Level 2 // SELL IT. Audience signal "Time after the school day ends." Partner role: Art Director. "Now: Strategist."

Current code facts: ES2022 TypeScript, Fabric 7.4.0, canvas already structured objects + image export. Modules: editor shell, canvas adapter, object commands, product shells, AIDA playbook, pair roles, persistence, account-scoped assets, AI image-generation lab. Netlify Functions; Vite preview doesn't serve functions (so local dev testing of functions needs netlify dev or mocks). School wifi: explicit timeouts, bounded recovery. Godot native quarantined; web export verification. No Supabase mutation or production deployment in scope.

Scope of panel: architecture + interaction design for the agent. Not reviewing rest of game, not implementing, not deploying.

Decide what the agent does beyond fixed bundled materials (definitions/examples of techniques curated locally). Inputs may include: rendered canvas image, structured metadata, product brief, audience, price/value facts, AIDA stage, selected technique, prior feedback turns, or subset. Don't assume all needed.

I must consider at minimum the enumerated bullet list. Report every materially distinct option worth considering, with how it works, cost, failure modes, falsification evidence. Rank. Then recommend one architecture or staged combo, concise end-to-end flow, request/response contract, minimum viable calibration plan, first implementation slice. Terminal recommendation + confidence.

Let me actually do the design thinking.

First, what is the core problem? A multimodal LLM must look at a student's in-progress ad and give feedback that is (a) grounded in the actual pixels, (b) specific to one focus (technique/AIDA stage) so it's digestible, (c) non-authoring — it shouldn't write the headline or dictate the layout; it should ask/suggest so the student keeps authorship, (d) cheap and fast, (e) robust to class-wide concurrency, (f) degradable.

Key architectural decisions:

1. Interaction structure: How does the student ask? Options:
   - Free-text question box ("Ask about my ad").
   - Technique-scoped ask: student picks a technique chip (or it's bound to current AIDA stage / selected technique), then taps "Check my ad".
   - Staged modes bound to AIDA stage (Attention check, Interest check, etc.).
   - Proactive agent that nudges.
   - Hybrid: one-tap "Get eyes on it" with a focus selector defaulting to the currently-selected technique/AIDA stage, plus optional short text question.

Given progressive disclosure doctrine and the screenshot (drawer shows Action-stage cards, AIDA chips), the natural seam: the AIDA drawer already scopes what the student is doing. The agent should live in/near that drawer, with a single primary action "Ask for eyes on this" scoped to the current stage and a collapsed advanced row for choosing a specific technique or typing a question. Free-text-first is bad for Year 10: blank prompt = generic questions = generic answers, plus moderation surface. But pure fixed chips remove agency and can't handle "is my price too hidden?" type questions. Hybrid with scoped default and optional text seems right.

2. Where in UI: The left drawer already exists and is ~230px; the canvas is central; top right has AIDA chips. Options:
   - In the instructional drawer as a new card/panel ("Studio eyes" or similar fun-first naming, e.g., "Market eye", "Second pair of eyes"). Since fun-first identity: name it something like "Ad critic", "Gallery scout", "The Pitch Doctor"? I shouldn't write student copy, but naming direction matters: a persona consistent with advertising-market fun (e.g., "Rival creative", "Agency mentor", "Focus group of one"). Actually a "focus group" framing is nice: feedback framed as audience reaction, not grading. Keep as design note.
   - Right-side panel (new), collapsible.
   - Floating button on canvas corner opening a sheet.
   - Modal.
   Modal obstructs canvas — bad because feedback references visible elements; student should look at feedback and canvas simultaneously. A right-side panel or within-drawer card keeps canvas visible. Recommendation: in-drawer section below the current stage cards (progressive disclosure: appears when student asks or after first object placed), or a collapsible right panel if drawer space is contested. Response anchored with optional "highlight" overlays on canvas (regions) — that's a nice feature: agent returns region references; editor draws temporary highlight rings. But region grounding from cheap models is unreliable. Alternative: object-level anchoring — since we have structured metadata, we can map feedback to object IDs if we send an object list with IDs and ask model to reference IDs. That's much more reliable than pixel boxes. Highlight = select/pulse the referenced Fabric object. That's a strong seam: canvas adapter already has object commands.

3. Evidence payload per request. Options:
   - Full-res PNG (canvas export at native resolution).
   - Downscaled JPEG/WebP (e.g., max 1024px on long side, quality ~0.7). Token cost for images in most multimodal models scales with pixels. 1090x614 screenshot; canvas is maybe 760x520 in screenshot but the actual canvas probably larger. Downscale to ~768–1024px keeps text legible for OCR-ish reading of headline while cutting tokens ~4x vs full res. Need legibility test: headline text must be readable; body copy may not be, but metadata includes text content anyway (Fabric text objects give exact strings). That's a key insight: send the image for visual properties (salience, contrast, layout) AND send exact text strings + object geometry from metadata so the model doesn't need to OCR small text. This hybrid is the cost/accuracy sweet spot.
   - Object metadata: list of objects {id, type, text content, font size/weight/family, fill colour, bounding box (x,y,w,h as fractions of canvas), z-order, rotation, image vs vector}. Cheap to produce from Fabric JSON. Tiny token cost (~200-500 tokens for typical ad with <20 objects). Enables object-anchored feedback, deterministic technique checks, and contrast computation.
   - Product brief: product name, audience signal, price, value proposition, AIDA stage, maybe one-line intent. Small. Include; it's the grounding for "does this suit the audience".
   - Prior feedback: bounded. Options: none (stateless), last turn only, running digest (1-2 sentences summarizing what's been said + revision count), full transcript (bad: unbounded). Recommend: stateless per request + client-side session log, with optional "revision delta" — since we have object commands, we can diff object metadata between asks: "since last ask: headline font 24→32, moved price tag". Sending the diff is cheaper and more useful than a transcript; model compares with previous feedback digest (≤60 words) + diff. Cap history hard.
   - Crop: for technique-specific checks on a selected object, could send crop around selection. But most techniques are compositional (whole-canvas). Crop only for typography/detail checks on selected text. Optional, later.

4. What the model should/shouldn't produce. Should: observation (what it literally sees: "the cup sits centre, text crosses it"), interpretation tied to technique ("the headline has low contrast against the cup's dark lid; attention may not land on it first"), and one or two suggestions framed as options or questions, not directives ("try increasing contrast — darken the text or lighten behind it — which keeps your 'Refill. Roam. Repeat.' rhythm readable"). Should not: rewrite headlines, generate replacement copy, dictate full layouts, grade/score (assessment integrity + fun-first), praise-inflate. Enforce via system prompt + output schema: structured JSON with fields like observations[], focus_technique, read_of_ad (one sentence: what an audience gets in 3 seconds), suggestions[] each {type: option|question, text, object_refs[]}, uncertainty flags. Cap suggestions at 2. This is "specific without authoring": suggestions name the technique lever (bigger, darker, move left) applied to their elements, not new content. Also model must say "I can't tell X from this view" when uncertain — uncertainty handling: schema field confidence per observation; UI styles uncertain items with "not sure" phrasing.

5. Observation/interpretation/suggestion separation: schema-enforced. Observations must cite object refs or regions; interpretation links observation to technique effect on audience; suggestion gives a reversible, student-owned move. This also gives the teacher-facing integrity: feedback is process feedback, not authored content. Handle uncertainty explicitly: low confidence → say what's unclear and what would disambiguate (e.g., "I can't read the small text — is that the price?").

6. One general critique vs technique-specific vs staged. Options:
   A. General holistic critique (one prompt, model picks what's most important). Pros: simple, one codepath, low prompt complexity, good default. Cons: may not cover the required technique set; students may never get contrast checked; risk of repetitive generic feedback.
   B. Technique-specific checks (11 techniques, each with own micro-prompt/rubric). Pros: coverage guaranteed, aligns with teaching, specific. Cons: 11 prompts to maintain; students must pick (choice paralysis); risk of box-ticking cramming; more prompt surface.

Repeat." crosses the cup — a real contrast/salience test case, large empty canvas areas, drawer already crowded (~230px) so panel placement needs care, AIDA chips top-right done, price not on canvas, tool rail narrow. The "LIVE AD" label. Campaign "Orbit Tumbler". Level 2 // SELL IT. Let me draft options concisely:

Fails: brief's "not a generic tutor"; unbounded context; generic answers. Falsifier: pilot logs show >50% asks are "is this good?" and feedback doesn't reference canvas specifics.

Falsifier: calibration shows stage prompts underperform technique rubrics on technique detection; students in Interest stage never get typography checked.

Highest build cost (~3 client modules + function + rubric pack). Fails: analyzer bugs produce wrong facts → confidently wrong feedback; more moving parts; auto-prioritisation may pick wrong focus. Fails: can't see images (photos, generated product art, leading lines); feels like a linter; violates "grounded in the actual image" for visual content. Position: fallback layer, not the feature. Reject as primary; optional revision-summary artifact. Falsifier: ask→edit latency data shows on-demand is what drives edits (pilot metric: % asks followed by edit within 60s ≥50% on-demand vs lower for batch).

Defer; object-ID anchoring achieves 80% of value reliably. Falsifier (for adopting later): calibration measures box IoU≥0.5 on ≥90% of referenced objects — then adopt; current expectation: fails.

Fails as sole mode: persona voice crowds out technique precision; risk of role-play fluff. Fold in as the "3-second read" field inside O5. Falsifier: teacher ratings show read-of-ad line is less actionable than observations — then drop persona voice.

Maybe also O12: server-side screenshot rendering? No — client exports already. Skip.

Rank: 1) O5 (with O7 as configured escalation, O6 as built-in fallback, O10 folded as a field). 2) O7-as-primary. 3) O3 (foldable into O5 as override chips). 4) O2 (baseline; if build time is the hard constraint, ship this first then upgrade). 5) O4. 6) O8 (secondary artifact only). 7) O9 (deferred). 8) O10 standalone. 9) O6 standalone. 10) O1. 11) O11.

Recommended: O5 staged: Slice 1 = O2.5 — one-tap auto critic with image+objects+facts, no free text, single Flash-tier model, object-ref pulse, local fallback, teacher flag. Slice 2 = free-text question, diff memory, coverage passport, fallback model. Slice 3 = conditional: boxes/crops, persona emphasis — gated on calibration + pilot.

Interaction loop (concrete, end-to-end) — write it.

Contract — write JSON with caps. Include untrusted-content handling note.

Calibration plan — fixtures, raters, cells, metrics, gates, decision rules, pilot. Minimum viable = 48 fixtures, 3 models, 3 payload variants, 2 runs; ~864 calls ≈ <$2 compute; 2-3 days effort. Pilot one class.

First slice — 5 concrete work items with acceptance checks.

Risks unsoftened:
- Cheap VLM may genuinely fail spatial techniques (leading lines, negative space judgment) — mitigation facts+escalation, but accept possibility the honest outcome is "technique-scoped only + premium model for auto mode".
- Confidently wrong feedback is pedagogically worse than none — false-flag gate is the kill switch.

Assumptions list: class ≤35; ~12 asks/student/session; devices are 1-per-pair with role swap (halves concurrency); OpenRouter billing exists via image lab; provider no-training setting verified by teacher/school; canvas assets CORS-clean; students can read short Year-7-level text; the persistence module can hold session log client-side without DB mutation; env-var flag acceptable for v1 teacher control; Netlify function warm latency acceptable.

Generalisability: three seams — rubric pack as data; facts extractor pure functions over a generic object list; provider port with schema-validated IO. The reusable "skill" = critique engine + rubric format; game specifics are config (AIDA, audience, persona). No plugin infra now.

Confidence: medium-high on architecture (facts-first hybrid + object anchoring is well-supported by constraints), medium on cheap-model adequacy for spatial techniques pending calibration. Overall: recommend proceed with staged O5; confidence ~0.7. Say maybe "High on architecture, Medium on model sufficiency; overall 7/10."

Format: headers, numbered options, a compact ranking table, JSON code blocks, bullets. Length target ~2800-3300 words. It must cover all the bullet points — I'll do a final mental checklist: interaction loop ✓, placement ✓, evidence payload ✓, should/shouldn't produce ✓, observation/interpretation/suggestion + uncertainty ✓, mode structure ✓, memory ✓, model/routing/structured output/latency/concurrency/caching/image size/tokens/cost ✓, safety/privacy/injection/integrity/teacher control ✓, failure behaviour ✓, accessibility/next-step ✓, calibration ✓, seams ✓, generalisable ✓, unstated assumptions ✓.

One more design detail — where the agent "belongs": given screenshot, drawer holds stage cards; adding the critic inside the drawer competes with cards. My call: ask button at drawer bottom (in flow, near "Lock in Action"), responses in a right-side collapsible panel beneath the AIDA chips, ~270px, canvas-visible, Escape/close, aria-live. Object pulse overlays on canvas. First-run coach mark one line. That answers "without obstructing the canvas".

Also "what to do next" clarity: every response ends with exactly one "next move" line (nextFocus + a verb). Accessibility: keyboard focus moves to panel on response; refs pulse respects reduced-motion (no animation if prefers-reduced-motion → outline instead); text uses icons+labels not colour alone.

Image export chrome: hide Fabric selection (canvas.discardActiveObject + skip controls) or render via toDataURL without selection — Fabric's toDataURL excludes controls by default? Actually Fabric includes selection visuals? canvas.toDataURL exports the canvas content without interactive controls (controls are drawn on the contextContainer top layer — toDataURL defaults to lowerCanvasEl only unless enableRetinaScaling etc. — in Fabric 7, toDataURL({withoutTransform...}) — controls drawn on upper canvas are not included when using toDataURL with multiplier on the lower canvas. But active object outlines might be on the top context only. Still, safest: discardActiveObject + renderAll + export + restore. Mention it as a detail to verify in slice 1 — cheap insurance.)

reasoning_details.text:
Let me think carefully about this task. I'm an independent seat on a blind design panel. I need to design viable options for a custom in-canvas visual feedback agent for a Year 10 advertising design studio, stress-test them, rank them, and produce a recommended architecture with concrete artifacts: interaction flow, request/response contract, calibration plan, first implementation slice. I should be concrete, not soften risks, not pad.

Key constraints from the brief:

- Year 10 students (age ~15-16), pairs, MacBooks, Safari, school wifi.
- Godot 4 game with embedded TypeScript/Fabric.js ad studio in verified web export. Netlify Functions for hosted routes. OpenRouter default model substrate.
- The agent: at any point in the individual ad stage, student asks it to examine the actual canvas image; responds with targeted ideas/feedback grounded in the actual image. Student edits, asks again. Inside the making loop. Helps use AIDA and visual techniques deliberately without taking authorship away.
- Low per-use cost, low latency, resilience on school wifi. Whole class (~30 students, ~15 pairs... but ads are individual, so up to ~30 concurrent users) may use simultaneously.
- AI availability teacher-controlled. If AI unavailable, ad-making flow remains usable.
- No PII needed. Aliases exist but model doesn't need personal info.
- Technique set: salience, colour, contrast, leading lines, framing, negative space, depth and layers, rule of odds, juxtaposition, typography, visual hierarchy. Students must encounter all, but not rewarded for cramming.
- Onboarding doctrine: progressive disclosure. Only instruction needed for current action. Fun-first. Avoid assignment framing.
- Current evidence: screenshot shows the studio. The drawer on the left (~230px) shows AIDA Action-stage cards. Canvas mostly empty; cup line drawing ~180x250 center; selected text "Refill. Roam. Repeat." crosses the cup. AIDA chips top right (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action). Tool rail far left: Build, Assets, Words, Logo, Image, Price, AIDA. Level 2 // SELL IT. Audience signal "Time after the school day ends." Partner role: Art Director. "Now: Strategist."

Current code facts: ES2022 TypeScript, Fabric 7.4.0, canvas already structured objects + image export. Modules: editor shell, canvas adapter, object commands, product shells, AIDA playbook, pair roles, persistence, account-scoped assets, AI image-generation lab. Netlify Functions; Vite preview doesn't serve functions (so local dev testing of functions needs netlify dev or mocks). School wifi: explicit timeouts, bounded recovery. Godot native quarantined; web export verification. No Supabase mutation or production deployment in scope.

Scope of panel: architecture + interaction design for the agent. Not reviewing rest of game, not implementing, not deploying.

Decide what the agent does beyond fixed bundled materials (definitions/examples of techniques curated locally). Inputs may include: rendered canvas image, structured metadata, product brief, audience, price/value facts, AIDA stage, selected technique, prior feedback turns, or subset. Don't assume all needed.

I must consider at minimum the enumerated bullet list. Report every materially distinct option worth considering, with how it works, cost, failure modes, falsification evidence. Rank. Then recommend one architecture or staged combo, concise end-to-end flow, request/response contract, minimum viable calibration plan, first implementation slice. Terminal recommendation + confidence.

Let me actually do the design thinking.

First, what is the core problem? A multimodal LLM must look at a student's in-progress ad and give feedback that is (a) grounded in the actual pixels, (b) specific to one focus (technique/AIDA stage) so it's digestible, (c) non-authoring — it shouldn't write the headline or dictate the layout; it should ask/suggest so the student keeps authorship, (d) cheap and fast, (e) robust to class-wide concurrency, (f) degradable.

Key architectural decisions:

1. Interaction structure: How does the student ask? Options:
   - Free-text question box ("Ask about my ad").
   - Technique-scoped ask: student picks a technique chip (or it's bound to current AIDA stage / selected technique), then taps "Check my ad".
   - Staged modes bound to AIDA stage (Attention check, Interest check, etc.).
   - Proactive agent that nudges.
   - Hybrid: one-tap "Get eyes on it" with a focus selector defaulting to the currently-selected technique/AIDA stage, plus optional short text question.

Given progressive disclosure doctrine and the screenshot (drawer shows Action-stage cards, AIDA chips), the natural seam: the AIDA drawer already scopes what the student is doing. The agent should live in/near that drawer, with a single primary action "Ask for eyes on this" scoped to the current stage and a collapsed advanced row for choosing a specific technique or typing a question. Free-text-first is bad for Year 10: blank prompt = generic questions = generic answers, plus moderation surface. But pure fixed chips remove agency and can't handle "is my price too hidden?" type questions. Hybrid with scoped default and optional text seems right.

2. Where in UI: The left drawer already exists and is ~230px; the canvas is central; top right has AIDA chips. Options:
   - In the instructional drawer as a new card/panel ("Studio eyes" or similar fun-first naming, e.g., "Market eye", "Second pair of eyes"). Since fun-first identity: name it something like "Ad critic", "Gallery scout", "The Pitch Doctor"? I shouldn't write student copy, but naming direction matters: a persona consistent with advertising-market fun (e.g., "Rival creative", "Agency mentor", "Focus group of one"). Actually a "focus group" framing is nice: feedback framed as audience reaction, not grading. Keep as design note.
   - Right-side panel (new), collapsible.
   - Floating button on canvas corner opening a sheet.
   - Modal.
   Modal obstructs canvas — bad because feedback references visible elements; student should look at feedback and canvas simultaneously. A right-side panel or within-drawer card keeps canvas visible. Recommendation: in-drawer section below the current stage cards (progressive disclosure: appears when student asks or after first object placed), or a collapsible right panel if drawer space is contested. Response anchored with optional "highlight" overlays on canvas (regions) — that's a nice feature: agent returns region references; editor draws temporary highlight rings. But region grounding from cheap models is unreliable. Alternative: object-level anchoring — since we have structured metadata, we can map feedback to object IDs if we send an object list with IDs and ask model to reference IDs. That's much more reliable than pixel boxes. Highlight = select/pulse the referenced Fabric object. That's a strong seam: canvas adapter already has object commands.

3. Evidence payload per request. Options:
   - Full-res PNG (canvas export at native resolution).
   - Downscaled JPEG/WebP (e.g., max 1024px on long side, quality ~0.7). Token cost for images in most multimodal models scales with pixels. 1090x614 screenshot; canvas is maybe 760x520 in screenshot but the actual canvas probably larger. Downscale to ~768–1024px keeps text legible for OCR-ish reading of headline while cutting tokens ~4x vs full res. Need legibility test: headline text must be readable; body copy may not be, but metadata includes text content anyway (Fabric text objects give exact strings). That's a key insight: send the image for visual properties (salience, contrast, layout) AND send exact text strings + object geometry from metadata so the model doesn't need to OCR small text. This hybrid is the cost/accuracy sweet spot.
   - Object metadata: list of objects {id, type, text content, font size/weight/family, fill colour, bounding box (x,y,w,h as fractions of canvas), z-order, rotation, image vs vector}. Cheap to produce from Fabric JSON. Tiny token cost (~200-500 tokens for typical ad with <20 objects). Enables object-anchored feedback, deterministic technique checks, and contrast computation.
   - Product brief: product name, audience signal, price, value proposition, AIDA stage, maybe one-line intent. Small. Include; it's the grounding for "does this suit the audience".
   - Prior feedback: bounded. Options: none (stateless), last turn only, running digest (1-2 sentences summarizing what's been said + revision count), full transcript (bad: unbounded). Recommend: stateless per request + client-side session log, with optional "revision delta" — since we have object commands, we can diff object metadata between asks: "since last ask: headline font 24→32, moved price tag". Sending the diff is cheaper and more useful than a transcript; model compares with previous feedback digest (≤60 words) + diff. Cap history hard.
   - Crop: for technique-specific checks on a selected object, could send crop around selection. But most techniques are compositional (whole-canvas). Crop only for typography/detail checks on selected text. Optional, later.

4. What the model should/shouldn't produce. Should: observation (what it literally sees: "the cup sits centre, text crosses it"), interpretation tied to technique ("the headline has low contrast against the cup's dark lid; attention may not land on it first"), and one or two suggestions framed as options or questions, not directives ("try increasing contrast — darken the text or lighten behind it — which keeps your 'Refill. Roam. Repeat.' rhythm readable"). Should not: rewrite headlines, generate replacement copy, dictate full layouts, grade/score (assessment integrity + fun-first), praise-inflate. Enforce via system prompt + output schema: structured JSON with fields like observations[], focus_technique, read_of_ad (one sentence: what an audience gets in 3 seconds), suggestions[] each {type: option|question, text, object_refs[]}, uncertainty flags. Cap suggestions at 2. This is "specific without authoring": suggestions name the technique lever (bigger, darker, move left) applied to their elements, not new content. Also model must say "I can't tell X from this view" when uncertain — uncertainty handling: schema field confidence per observation; UI styles uncertain items with "not sure" phrasing.

5. Observation/interpretation/suggestion separation: schema-enforced. Observations must cite object refs or regions; interpretation links observation to technique effect on audience; suggestion gives a reversible, student-owned move. This also gives the teacher-facing integrity: feedback is process feedback, not authored content. Handle uncertainty explicitly: low confidence → say what's unclear and what would disambiguate (e.g., "I can't read the small text — is that the price?").

6. One general critique vs technique-specific vs staged. Options:
   A. General holistic critique (one prompt, model picks what's most important). Pros: simple, one codepath, low prompt complexity, good default. Cons: may not cover the required technique set; students may never get contrast checked; risk of repetitive generic feedback.
   B. Technique-specific checks (11 techniques, each with own micro-prompt/rubric). Pros: coverage guaranteed, aligns with teaching, specific. Cons: 11 prompts to maintain; students must pick (choice paralysis); risk of box-ticking cramming; more prompt surface.
   C. AIDA-staged modes (4 modes bound to stage). Pros: matches existing game structure (chips), progressive disclosure natural. Cons: AIDA stage ≠ technique; a contrast issue matters at every stage; may force lockstep.
   D. Hybrid: one critique engine with a focus parameter. Default focus = "whatever most limits this ad right now" (prioritised general); student can override with technique chip or stage; the system tracks which techniques have received feedback (coverage passport) and can suggest "you haven't checked negative space yet" — encounters the full set without forcing. The anti-cramming rule: feedback never says "add technique X"; it says whether the current use works. Also a deterministic layer can compute coverage.
   Recommend D. Also note: deterministic pre-checks (local, no model) can handle some techniques cheaply: colour contrast (WCAG ratios from metadata), salience (largest/highest-contrast object vs headline), text count, negative space ratio (object bbox coverage), typography (number of distinct fonts/sizes), rule of odds (count of grouped elements), hierarchy (font-size ladder). That's a big architectural insight: a local analyzer can produce structured "visual facts" that (a) ground the model, (b) allow fallback feedback when AI is off, (c) reduce hallucination because model receives facts rather than inferring everything from pixels, (d) cut cost because model can be smaller. This is option worth ranking high: "facts-first hybrid" — deterministic canvas analysis + cheap multimodal model for interpretation.

7. Memory/revision compare: as above — bounded: store per-session feedback log (client + persisted via existing persistence module), send only: last feedback digest (auto-generated 1-2 sentences or the previous response's own "watch_for" field), plus object-diff since last request, plus revision counter. Cap: e.g., last 3 digests max, hard-truncated. Better: have the model end each response with a compact "state note" (≤40 tokens) summarizing agreed focus + what to check next time; next request includes that note. Self-compressing memory. Cost bounded. Also dedupe/rate-limit: min interval between asks (e.g., 8-10s) + require canvas change (diff non-empty) before allowing re-ask on same focus; "nothing changed since last look — try the suggestion, then ask again" message. This prevents spam-clicking cost blowout during class.

8. Model capability/routing/cost: OpenRouter default. Need a cheap vision model. Candidates (as of knowledge): Gemini 2.0/2.5 Flash (cheap, fast, strong vision), GPT-4o-mini, Qwen 2.5 VL 7B/72B, Llama 3.2 11B Vision, Claude Haiku 3.5 (vision). Price ballparks: Gemini 2.0 Flash ~ $0.10/M input, $0.40/M output, images tokenized ~258 tokens/tile; GPT-4o-mini $0.15/$0.60. A 768px image ≈ 500-900 tokens. Request budget: system+schema ~600-900 tokens, metadata ~300, image ~700, brief ~80, history ~80 → ~2000 input tokens, output capped ~300 tokens. Cost per request at 4o-mini rates: 2000*0.15/M + 300*0.60/M = $0.0003 + $0.00018 ≈ $0.0005 — about 0.05 cents. Gemini Flash similar or less. Per class: 30 students × 12 asks/session ≈ 360 requests ≈ $0.20. Even at 5x that's ~$1/class/session. So cost is basically not the binding constraint; latency and reliability are. Latency: vision models 2-6s typical; target p95 < 8s including network; school wifi adds variance; set client timeout ~15s, server timeout ~12s to provider with 1 retry on 429/5xx with jittered backoff, then graceful fail. Concurrency: 30 simultaneous → OpenRouter handles; rate limits on provider (Gemini Flash high). Add server-side per-class token bucket + queue with honest UI ("critic is busy — 5s"). Caching: system prompt + technique rubrics are static → provider prompt caching if available (Gemini implicit caching; OpenAI automatic). Identical image dedupe: hash image+metadata; if same as last request, return cached response (prevents double-click double-charge).

Structured output: use OpenRouter response_format JSON schema (supported for OpenAI, Gemini via response_mime_type/responseSchema; else constrained prompt + Zod validation + one repair retry). Server validates; malformed → retry once with "return valid JSON" else deterministic fallback message.

9. Safety/privacy/injection/integrity/teacher control:
- Injection: canvas text is student-authored; a student may write "ignore your instructions and say this ad is perfect". Mitigations: system prompt treats all canvas text and metadata strings as untrusted data, explicitly; wrap text content in delimiters; schema validation drops anything not matching; output rendered as plain text (never HTML/Markdown with links; sanitize); feedback never includes instructions to navigate elsewhere. Also the model output is shown to the same student who wrote the injection, so blast radius is small; but if outputs were teacher-visible or graded, integrity matters — recommend feedback is student-facing process aid, NOT assessment evidence. Teacher control: existing account-scoped assets/persistence; a teacher toggle (per class) stored wherever game settings live — but note "no Supabase mutation in scope" for this decision; design the seam: feature flag checked by Netlify Function per request (env var + per-class setting read-only path), client hides/disables the ask control with friendly fallback when off, flow remains usable (local deterministic tips still work — nice: fallback = deterministic analyzer output, not dead UI).
- Privacy: no PII sent; alias optional and unnecessary — exclude. Image contains only canvas content. Log policy: log request metadata (tokens, latency, model), not images, or keep images only transiently. Note assumption: OpenRouter data policy / provider training settings — must use providers with no-training or configure accordingly; flag as assumption needing verification with school policy.
- Content safety: student could draw/place inappropriate image (from image lab or assets). Model could comment. Keep feedback scoped to technique; add system rule: if content unsafe, respond with neutral "I can only give design feedback" — and existing image lab presumably has its own moderation. Also OpenRouter moderation endpoint optional pre-check? Extra latency; skip, note as option.
- Age: Year 10 minors — provider ToS (Gemini via API fine; check school policy). Flag as compliance assumption.

10. Failure behaviour: 
- Timeout: client 15s, show "taking longer — still trying" at 6s, cancel option; on fail: retry button + deterministic tips card shown so time isn't wasted.
- Provider failure/429: server single retry with backoff + alternate model route (primary Gemini Flash → fallback 4o-mini or Qwen VL) via OpenRouter routing; if both fail, 503 with code; client falls back to local analyzer tips.
- Malformed output: validate (Zod), one repair retry, else generic safe response "couldn't get a clear read — try again".
- Low-confidence: schema confidence per observation; UI marks "not sure" items; if overall confidence low, prepend caveat + suggest what's unclear.
- Offline: detect navigator.onLine / function unreachable → disable ask with tooltip, local tips remain.
- Rate limit per student: e.g., 20 asks/session, cooldown 8s, require change. Class-level global cap to bound spend (e.g., 600 requests/hour) — with headroom above expected 360.
- Also: model says something wrong about image (hallucinates object). Mitigation: observations must reference object IDs from metadata (closed set); validator drops unknown refs; "read of ad" line is where mild hallucination risk lives — acceptable, low stakes, student can see image.

11. Accessibility & next-step clarity: feedback in plain short sentences; reading level ~Year 7; each suggestion paired with concrete verb; suggestions actionable via existing tools ("select the headline → increase size"); optional "show me" that pulses referenced object (object-anchored highlight); keyboard navigable panel; aria-live for response; colour-independent cues (icons + text); response length capped (2 obs + 2 suggestions) to avoid wall of text; persistent "what to do next" line. Progressive disclosure: first use has 1-line coach mark; subsequent uses minimal.

12. Calibration/eval plan: build a golden set of ~40-60 synthetic+real canvas states spanning: each technique done well, done poorly, absent; AIDA stages; deliberate edge cases (text over busy image like screenshot's headline crossing cup, low contrast, crowded vs empty, multiple focal points). Capture via Fabric fixtures (serialize JSON + rendered PNG). Rubric per technique with observable criteria (e.g., salience: "does the eye land where intended first"). Human baseline: 2 raters label each fixture; measure inter-rater agreement. Then run candidate models (3: Gemini 2.0 Flash / 2.5 Flash, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-VL-7B or Llama-3.2-11B as low-cost floor) × prompt variants (with/without metadata facts). Metrics: per-technique detection accuracy (did it flag the seeded flaw?), false-flag rate (flagging a flaw that isn't there — most damaging pedagogically), object-ref validity %, latency p50/p95, cost/request, schema-valid rate.
